context: Uranium-zirconium-oxide oxidized particles; extra-stable matrix; zirconium alloy cladding fragments incorporated
notes: Most resistant to dissolution; 31 ± 4% of radionuclide activities in Red Forest waste (2015); U-Zry-Ox particles persist longest in environment
source: Kashparov 2020 J Environ Radioact PMID:31419762; Levchuk 2020 PMID:32868094

context: Non-oxidized uranium oxide matrix; chemically stable but less so than Type I; primary fuel pellet material
notes: ~50% of Type II particles had dissolved by 1999-2005 in surface soils; slower dissolution rate in flooded/anoxic conditions
source: Kashparov 2004 J Environ Radioact PMID:14972414; Kashparov 1999 PMID:10025650

context: Oxidized uranium oxide; low chemical stability; most reactive type; formed at high temperatures in oxidizing conditions
notes: Complete dissolution by 1999-2005 in near-zone surface soils; dissolution 7-10x faster than Type II; dominant in early releases

context: Exposed surface soils; pH 5.5-7; aerobic conditions
notes: Most stable particles; dissolution accelerates with increasing pH and oxidizing conditions; Red Forest waste shows highest type I fraction

context: Surface agricultural soils; aerobic; temperate climate
notes: ~50% dissolved by year 2000 (14 years post-accident); dissolution rate strongly pH and oxidation dependent

context: Surface soils; oxidizing conditions
notes: Fastest dissolution; effectively all Type III dissolved by ~1995-2000 in most near-zone soils
source: Kashparov 2004 PMID:14972414; dissolution model validation Levchuk 2020

context: Oxidized vs non-oxidized UO2 particles in identical soil conditions
notes: Oxidation state of fuel particle is primary determinant of dissolution rate; more oxidized = faster dissolution = faster radionuclide release to soil solution

context: Cooling pond sediment vs surface soil; anoxic reducing conditions
notes: Near-field cooling pond: ~100 years for substantial dissolution vs 15-25 years in exposed sediments; groundwater Sr-90 contamination driven by slow dissolution

context: Individual fuel crystallites and grain fragments; most common size mode
notes: Bimodal distribution: fine mode 0.3-1.5 µm AMAD (volatile: I Cs); coarse mode ~10 µm (refractory: Pu Zr Ce); particles >20 µm can transport hundreds of km
source: Salbu 2001 J Environ Radioact PMID:11202686; OECD-NEA Ch.II

context: Largest fuel fragments observed in near-zone soil samples (within 1-5 km)
notes: Large particles carry highest activity per particle; inhalation of particles >20 µm mostly deposits in upper respiratory tract; smaller particles reach lungs
source: Kashparov 2003 Environ Sci Pollut Res; Salbu 2001

context: Fine mode particles containing volatile elements (I Cs Te) in aerosol; AMAD = aerodynamic median activity diameter
notes: Fine mode carries 10-20% of total activity; penetrates to lung alveoli if inhaled; dominant exposure pathway for distant populations (>100 km)

context: Refractory elements Pu Zr Ce Ba; mainly near-source deposit; captured in upper respiratory tract if inhaled
notes: Coarse particles carry 80-90% of non-volatile radionuclide activity; near-zone inhalation dose dominated by coarse mode

context: Near-zone fuel particles 1-30 km from reactor; extremely wide range reflecting size range
notes: Larger fragments = higher activity; very large pieces could deliver acute local doses; most particles in resuspended aerosol: 1-12 Bq Cs-137 per particle

context: Fuel hot particles in resuspended aerosol in 30-km zone; measured by Salbu 2001
notes: Individual hot particle inhalation dose: typical particle gives <0.001 mSv committed lung dose; large particles (>100 µm) could give locally concentrated dose but not systemically significant

context: Ru-enriched condensate particles from volatile ruthenium species; found predominantly in far-zone
notes: Ruthenium particles distinct from fuel particles; condensate droplets formed at different temperatures; Ru-106 (and Ru-103) co-presence distinguishes from 2017 European Ru event

context: Wind-driven resuspension in 30-km zone; agricultural activities
notes: Agricultural activities resuspend 36 particles per 1000 m³ (14x wind resuspension); wildfire resuspension substantially higher; key ongoing exposure pathway in CEZ

context: CEZ agricultural activity (ploughing tilling); measured geometric diameter 6-12 µm
notes: Farming in CEZ (now partially resumed) creates hot particle inhalation hazard; 100 hectares declared safe for agriculture 2025 after individual validation

context: Upper 30 cm of 30-km exclusion zone soil; decay-corrected to year 2000
notes: Sr-90 higher mobility than Cs-137 in soils; significant fraction moves to groundwater; Bugai 2022 measured CEZ groundwater Sr-90 still elevated; ~15% may be in particle form

context: Upper 30 cm of 30-km exclusion zone soil; decay-corrected to year 2000
notes: Cs-137 strongly fixed in clay minerals in agricultural soils (low mobility); forest soils: less fixation → higher bioavailability → mushroom and wildlife contamination

context: Upper 30 cm of 30-km exclusion zone soil; decay-corrected to year 2000
notes: Plutonium isotopes highly insoluble; essentially no soil-to-plant transfer; primary exposure via inhalation of dust/particles near reactor

context: Upper 30 cm of 30-km exclusion zone soil; year 2000
notes: Pu-239 t1/2=24110yr: essentially permanent contamination on human timescales; hot spot within 30km zone: >37 kBq/m2 Pu-239+240 in ~800 km2

context: Upper 30 cm of 30-km exclusion zone soil; year 2000; Am-241 still growing from Pu-241 ingrowth
notes: Am-241 in soil year 2000 includes both direct release (from 1986) + ingrowth from deposited Pu-241; by 2026 ingrowth component greatly exceeds original release

context: 50-km zone soil samples 1995-1997; represents fraction not yet dissolved into exchangeable/mobile form
notes: At year 1997 (11 years post-accident) 2-21% of Sr-90 still in fuel particle matrix; remainder dissolved and variably sorbed; particle dissolution the slow-release source term for groundwater

context: Red Forest waste samples 2015 (29 years post-accident); Type I particles dominant in this high-contamination area
notes: 31 ± 4% Sr-90 still in most-stable (Type I U-Zry-Ox) particle matrix after 29 years; these particles are the long-term persistent source; will take additional decades to fully dissolve

context: Western trace zone podzolic soils pH 6.0; lower pH slows dissolution; 2016 measurements
notes: Soil pH strongly controls dissolution rate; podzolic acidic soils (~pH 5-6) retain more activity in particle form than neutral pH agricultural soils; important for groundwater modeling

context: At time of deposition April-May 1986; decay-corrected to May 6 1986 = 0.57
notes: Unique Chernobyl temporal fingerprint; Cs-134 t1/2=2.065yr; by 1990 ratio ~0.25; by 1994 ratio ~0.06; by 2000 essentially zero → all remaining Cs-137 must be Chernobyl not Cs-134 decay distinguishable

context: Near-zone soils 2-5 km from reactor; fuel particle dominated contamination
notes: Wide ratio reflects mixture of fuel particles (higher Cs/Sr ratio) vs condensation fallout; ratio used to characterize degree of fuel vs condensate contamination at measurement site

context: Activity ratio at time of release April-May 1986; both fuel-associated radionuclides
notes: Zr-95/Ce-144 = ~0.73 ± 0.05 at release (Kashparov); ratio used with age-of-particle model to date particle age; both nuclides decayed by ~1990 so only useful in historical samples

context: Typical inhalable hot particle 1-12 Bq Cs-137; lung dose from single particle inhalation
notes: Individual hot particle inhalation: negligible systemic dose; however localized microdosimetry to single alveolus may be very high (debated in literature as mechanism of carcinogenesis)

context: IAEA distinguishes Type 1 contamination (dissolved/exchangeable) from Type 2 (particle-bound); different dose pathways
notes: Type 2 (particle-bound) = inhalation/ingestion of intact particles; more localized dose to lung/GI; Type 1 (dissolved) = systemic distribution via blood; thyroid (I) bone (Sr) whole body (Cs) dose patterns
